'''Svante Pääbo''' ({{IPA|sv|ˈsvânːtɛ̂ ˈpʰɛ̌ːbʊ̂|lang}};<ref>{{cite AV media |people=Lena Nordlund, Annlouise Martin (Producers) |date=14 August 2014 |title=Svante Pääbo |medium=Radio |url=https://sverigesradio.se/avsnitt/svante-paabo#75 |access-date=2 May 2018 |format=MP3 |publisher=[[Sveriges Radio]] |time=1:15 |archive-date=3 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221003125237/https://sverigesradio.se/avsnitt/svante-paabo#75 |url-status=live}}</ref> born 20 April 1955) is a Swedish [[geneticist]] and Nobel Laureate who specialises in the field of [[Extended evolutionary synthesis|evolutionary genetics]].<ref name="gs">{{Google Scholar ID}}</ref> As one of the founders of [[paleogenetics]], he has worked extensively on the [[Neanderthal genome]].<ref name=kolbert>{{cite magazine |last=Kolbert |first=Elizabeth |author-link=Elizabeth Kolbert |title=Sleeping with the Enemy: What happened between the Neanderthals and us? |magazine=[[The New Yorker]] |issue=15 & 22 August 2011 |pages=64–75 |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2011/08/15/sleeping-with-the-enemy |access-date=23 November 2021 |archive-date=11 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220711123151/https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2011/08/15/sleeping-with-the-enemy |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=lostgenomes /> In 1997, he became founding director of the Department of Genetics at the [[Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology]] in [[Leipzig]], Germany.<ref>{{Cite journal
| last1 = Gitschier | first1 = J.
| title = Imagine: An Interview with Svante Pääbo
| doi = 10.1371/journal.pgen.1000035
| journal = [[PLOS Genetics]]
| publisher=[[PLOS]]
| volume = 4
| issue = 3
| article-number = e1000035
| year = 2008
| pmid = 18369454
| pmc =2274957
| doi-access = free
}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Zagorski | first1 = N. | title = Profile of Svante Pääbo| doi = 10.1073/pnas.0606596103 | journal = [[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]]| volume = 103 | issue = 37 | pages = 13575–13577 | year = 2006 | pmid = 16954182| pmc = 1564240| bibcode = 2006PNAS..10313575Z | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://wwwstaff.eva.mpg.de/~paabo/|title=Svante Paabo at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology|access-date=27 July 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719062916/http://wwwstaff.eva.mpg.de/~paabo/|archive-date=19 July 2011}}</ref> Since 1999, he has been an honorary professor at [[Leipzig University]]; he currently teaches molecular evolutionary biology at the university.<ref name="Heckmann2020">{{cite web |last1=Heckmann |first1=Carsten |title=Honorary professor at Leipzig University recognised: Japan Prize Goes to Svante Pääbo |url=https://www.uni-leipzig.de/en/newsdetail/artikel/japan-prize-goes-to-svante-paeaebo-2020-02-10 |website=Leipzig University |date=10 February 2020 |publisher=eipzig University |access-date=17 October 2022 |archive-date=17 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221017133820/https://www.uni-leipzig.de/en/newsdetail/artikel/japan-prize-goes-to-svante-paeaebo-2020-02-10 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Heckmann2022">{{cite web |last1=Heckmann |first1=Carsten |title=Congratulations to our honorary professor! Nobel Prize for Savante Pääbo |url=https://www.uni-leipzig.de/en/newsdetail/artikel/nobel-prize-for-svante-paeaebo-2022-10-04 |website=Leipzig University |date=4 October 2022 |publisher=eipzig University |access-date=17 October 2022 |archive-date=17 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221017133821/https://www.uni-leipzig.de/en/newsdetail/artikel/nobel-prize-for-svante-paeaebo-2022-10-04 |url-status=live }}</ref> He is also an adjunct professor at [[Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology]], Japan.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://groups.oist.jp/heg/svante-paeaebo|title=Svante Pääbo|date=29 April 2020|website=OIST Groups|access-date=3 October 2022|archive-date=24 October 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211024000436/https://groups.oist.jp/heg/svante-paeaebo|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2022, he was awarded the [[Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine]] "for his discoveries concerning the genomes of extinct hominins and human evolution".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2022/press-release/|title=Press release: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2022|access-date=3 October 2022|archive-date=3 October 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221003134750/https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2022/summary/?_pjax=%23pjax-well|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="ReutersNobel">{{cite news |last1=Grover |first1=Natalie |last2=Pollard |first2=Niklas |last3=Ahlander |first3=Johan |title=Swedish geneticist wins Nobel medicine prize for decoding ancient DNA |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/svante-paabo-wins-2022-nobel-prize-medicine-2022-10-03/ |access-date=3 October 2022 |publisher=[[Reuters]] |date=3 October 2022 |archive-date=3 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221003101314/https://www.reuters.com/world/svante-paabo-wins-2022-nobel-prize-medicine-2022-10-03/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=6 October 2022 |title=Nobel laureate Svante Paabo's ancient DNA discoveries shed light on what makes us human |url=https://www.onmanorama.com/news/world/2022/10/04/nobel-prize-winner-svante-paabo-ancient-dna-discoveries.html |access-date=6 October 2022 |website=Onmanorama |language=en |archive-date=6 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221006042400/https://www.onmanorama.com/news/world/2022/10/04/nobel-prize-winner-svante-paabo-ancient-dna-discoveries.html |url-status=live}}</ref>

== Education and early life ==
Pääbo was born in Stockholm, Sweden, in 1955 and grew up there with his mother,<ref name=kolbert /> [[Republic of Estonia|Estonian]] chemist Karin Pääbo ({{IPA|et|ˈpæːpo|lang}}; 1925–2013), who had escaped from the [[Tallinn offensive|Soviet invasion]] in 1944<ref name="Eesti Päevaleht">{{cite news|author1=Külli Riin Tigasson|url=https://epl.delfi.ee/artikkel/64086549/taismahus-svante-paabo-mis-tegi-inimesest-inimese?|title=Svante Pääbo: mis tegi inimesest inimese?|access-date=20 October 2022|work=Eesti Päevaleht|date=17 March 2012|format=Interview with subject|language=et|archive-date=21 October 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221021133625/https://epl.delfi.ee/artikkel/64086549/taismahus-svante-paabo-mis-tegi-inimesest-inimese|url-status=live}}</ref> and arrived in Sweden as a refugee during World War II.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Tambur |first1=Silver |title=Estonian descendant Svante Pääbo awarded Nobel prize |url=https://estonianworld.com/knowledge/estonian-descendant-svante-paabo-awarded-a-nobel-prize/ |website=EstonianWorld |access-date=8 October 2022 |language=en |date=3 October 2022 |archive-date=8 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221008180732/https://estonianworld.com/knowledge/estonian-descendant-svante-paabo-awarded-a-nobel-prize/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Strandberg |first1=Marek |title=Eesti juurtega Svante Pääbo tõi kärgperre teisegi Nobeli auhinna |url=https://teadus.postimees.ee/7618998/eesti-juurtega-svante-paabo-toi-kargperre-teisegi-nobeli-auhinna |work=Postimees |date=4 October 2022 |language=et |access-date=18 October 2022 |archive-date=18 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221018173355/https://teadus.postimees.ee/7618998/eesti-juurtega-svante-paabo-toi-kargperre-teisegi-nobeli-auhinna |url-status=live }}{{subscription required}}</ref> He was born through an extramarital affair<ref>{{cite web |last1=Schultz |first1=Isaac |title=Paleogeneticist Svante Pääbo Picks Up Nobel Prize for Human Origins Research |url=https://gizmodo.com/svante-paabo-nobel-prize-human-origins-neanderthals-1849609090 |website=Gizmodo |access-date=6 October 2022 |language=en |date=3 October 2022 |archive-date=6 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221006135922/https://gizmodo.com/svante-paabo-nobel-prize-human-origins-neanderthals-1849609090 |url-status=live }}</ref> of his father, Swedish biochemist [[Sune Bergström]] (1916–2004),<ref name=kolbert /> who, like his son, became a recipient of the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (in 1982).<ref name=forbes /> Pääbo is his mother's only child; he has via his father's marriage a half-brother, Rurik Reenstierna (also born in 1955), who only learned Svante was his brother in 2004.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dn.se/sverige/svante-paabo-far-nobelpriset-i-medicin/|title=Svensken Svante Pääbo får Nobelpriset i medicin|date=3 October 2022|website=Dagens Nyheter|access-date=3 October 2022|archive-date=3 October 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221003101930/https://www.dn.se/sverige/svante-paabo-far-nobelpriset-i-medicin/|url-status=live |language=sv}}</ref>

Pääbo later described his childhood as:<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2022/paabo/podcast/|title=Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2022|website=NobelPrize.org}}</ref>
{{Quote|text=First of all, I grew up as a single child of a single mum. Our father only visited us on Saturdays for a few hours. I think my mum was a very strong woman who took my interest seriously too. When I got interested in runic stones, we would on Saturdays and Sundays drive around and look at runic stones around Stockholm and I would measure them and copy the runes. She really took time to sort of nurture those interests.}}

Pääbo grew up as a native Swedish speaker.<ref name="Eesti Päevaleht"/> In a 2012 interview with the Estonian newspaper ''[[Eesti Päevaleht]]'', he said that he self-identifies as a [[Swedes|Swede]], but has a "special relationship with Estonia".<ref>{{cite news|author1=Külli Riin Tigasson|url=https://epl.delfi.ee/artikkel/64086549/taismahus-svante-paabo-mis-tegi-inimesest-inimese?|title=Svante Pääbo: mis tegi inimesest inimese?|access-date=20 October 2022|work=Eesti Päevaleht|date=17 March 2012|format=Interview with subject|quote=Pääbo was quoted saying: "I grew up understanding what Estonia is, but I don't speak Estonian. I have never attended Estonian school. I identify with the Swedes, but I have a special relationship with Estonia."(''Kasvasin üles teades, mis on Eesti, aga eesti keelt ma ei räägi. Ma pole kunagi käinud eesti koolis. Identifitseerin end rootslastega, aga mul on eriline suhe Eestiga'')|language=et|archive-date=21 October 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221021133625/https://epl.delfi.ee/artikkel/64086549/taismahus-svante-paabo-mis-tegi-inimesest-inimese|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 1975, Pääbo began studying at [[Uppsala University]], serving one year in the Swedish Defense Forces attached to the School of Interpreters. Pääbo earned his Ph.D. from Uppsala University in 1986 for research investigating how the E19 [[protein]] of [[adenovirus]]es modulates the [[immune system]].<ref name=phd>{{cite thesis |degree=PhD |first=Svante |last=Pääbo |title=How the E19 protein of adenoviruses modulates the immune system |publisher=Uppsala University |year=1986 |url=http://urn.kb.se/resolve?urn=urn%3Anbn%3Ase%3Auu%3Adiva-114617 |oclc=16668494 |isbn=91-554-1921-6 |access-date=22 December 2016 |archive-date=3 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221003134617/http://uu.diva-portal.org/smash/record.jsf?pid=diva2%3A294502&dswid=261 |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Research and career ==
[[File:SvantePääbo.jpg|thumb|left|200px|Pääbo at the 2014 [[Nobel Conference]]]]

Pääbo is known as one of the founders of [[paleogenetics]], a discipline that uses [[genetics]] to study [[early humans]] and other ancient species.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/entrez?db=pubmed&cmd=search&term=Paabo%20S |title=Svante Paabo publications in PubMed |access-date=27 July 2011 |archive-date=3 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221003134602/https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?cmd=search&term=Paabo+S |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.edge.org/3rd_culture/paabo09/paabo09_index.html |title=Edge: Mapping the Neanderthal Genome – A Conversation With Svante Pääbo |access-date=27 July 2011 |archive-date=13 December 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121213032155/http://www.edge.org/3rd_culture/paabo09/paabo09_index.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

From 1986 to 1987, he did postdoctoral research at the Institute for Molecular Biology II, [[University of Zurich]], Switzerland.<ref name="MaxPlanch">{{cite web|title=Svante Pääbo|url=https://gizmodo.com/svante-paabo-nobel-prize-human-origins-neanderthals-1849609090|website=Max Planch Institute|date=3 October 2022|language=en|access-date=6 October 2022|archive-date=6 October 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221006135922/https://gizmodo.com/svante-paabo-nobel-prize-human-origins-neanderthals-1849609090|url-status=live}}</ref>

As an [[European Molecular Biology Organization|EMBO]] Postdoctoral Fellow, Pääbo moved to the United States in 1987, accepting a position as a postdoctoral researcher in biochemistry at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he joined [[Allan Wilson (biologist)|Allan Wilson]]'s lab and worked on the genome of extinct mammals.<ref name=MaxPlanch/><ref name=SciAm>{{cite web|author=Daniela Mocker|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/nobel-winner-svante-paeaebo-discovered-the-neandertal-in-our-genes/|title=Nobel Winner Svante Pääbo Discovered the Neandertal in Our Genes|website=Scientific American|date=4 October 2022|access-date=17 October 2022|archive-date=17 October 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221017201936/https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/nobel-winner-svante-paeaebo-discovered-the-neandertal-in-our-genes/|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 1990, he returned to Europe to become professor of general biology at [[LMU Munich]], and, in 1997, he became founding director of the [[Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology]] in Leipzig, Germany.<ref name=SciAm/>

In 1997, Pääbo and colleagues reported their successful sequencing of [[Neanderthal]] mitochondrial DNA ([[mtDNA]]), originating from a [[Biological specimen|specimen]] found in [[Kleine Feldhofer Grotte|Feldhofer grotto]] in the [[Neandertal (valley)|Neander valley]].<ref>{{Cite journal|pmid=9230299 |year=1997 |author1=Krings, M |author2=Stone, A |author3=Schmitz, Rw |author4=Krainitzki, H |author5=Stoneking, M |author6=Pääbo, S |title=Neandertal DNA sequences and the origin of modern humans |volume=90 |issue=1 |pages=19–30 |issn=0092-8674 |journal=Cell |doi=10.1016/S0092-8674(00)80310-4|hdl=11858/00-001M-0000-0025-0960-8 |s2cid=13581775 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Rincon 2018">{{cite web| last=Rincon| first=Paul| title=How ancient DNA is transforming our view of the past| publisher=BBC| date=11 April 2018| url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-43701630| access-date=11 April 2018| archive-date=30 March 2019| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190330164316/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-43701630| url-status=live}}</ref>

In August 2002, Pääbo's department published findings about the "language gene", [[FOXP2]], which is mutated in some individuals with language disabilities.<ref>{{Cite journal

In 2006, Pääbo announced a plan to reconstruct the entire genome of Neanderthals. In 2007, he was named one of ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' magazine's 100 most influential people of the year.<ref>{{Cite magazine
| last1 = Venter | first1 = J. C.
| title = Time 100 scientists & thinkers. Svante Paabo
| magazine = Time
| volume = 169
| issue = 20
| page = 116
| year = 2007
| pmid = 17536326
}}</ref>

In February 2009, at the Annual Meeting of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (AAAS) in Chicago, it was announced that the [[Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology]] had completed the first draft version of the [[Neanderthal genome]].<ref>Callaway, Ewen (12 February 2009) [https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn16587-first-draft-of-neanderthal-genome-is-unveiled.html#.VN4-s1JyZ7h First draft of Neanderthal genome is unveiled] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221003134749/https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn16587-first-draft-of-neanderthal-genome-is-unveiled/?ignored=irrelevant#.VN4-s1JyZ7h |date=3 October 2022 }} New Scientist, Life. Retrieved 13 February 2015.</ref> Over 3&nbsp;billion [[base pair]]s were sequenced in collaboration with the [[454 Life Sciences]] Corporation.<ref>{{Cite press release |date=12 February 2009 |title=Neanderthal genome completed |work=[[Max-Planck-Gesellschaft]] |url=https://www.mpg.de/591280/pressRelease200902111 |access-date=4 October 2022 |archive-date=27 November 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211127084713/https://www.mpg.de/591280/pressRelease200902111 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In March 2010, Pääbo and his coworkers published a report about the DNA analysis of a finger bone found in the [[Denisova Cave]] in [[Siberia]]; the results suggest that the [[bone]] belonged to an [[extinct]] member of the [[genus]] ''[[Homo]]'' that had not yet been recognised, the [[Denisova hominin]].<ref>{{Cite journal
| last1 = Krause | first1 = J.
| last2 = Fu | first2 = Q.
| last3 = Good | first3 = J. M.
| last4 = Viola | first4 = B.
| last5 = Shunkov | first5 = M. V.
| last6 = Derevianko | first6 = A. P.
| last7 = Pääbo | first7 = S.
| doi = 10.1038/nature08976
| title = The complete mitochondrial DNA genome of an unknown hominin from southern Siberia
| journal = Nature
| volume = 464
| issue = 7290
| pages = 894–897
| year = 2010
| pmid = 20336068
| pmc = 10152974
| bibcode = 2010Natur.464..894K
| doi-access = free
}}</ref> Pääbo first wanted to classify the Denisovans as a species of their own, separate from modern humans and Neanderthals but changed his mind after peer-review.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Karlsson |first=Mattis |url=http://urn.kb.se/resolve?urn=urn:nbn:se:liu:diva-182568 |title=From Fossil To Fact: The Denisova Discovery as Science in Action |date=18 February 2022 |publisher=Linköping University Electronic Press |isbn=978-91-7929-170-9 |series=Linköping Studies in Arts and Sciences |volume=830 |location=Linköping |language=en |doi=10.3384/9789179291716 |s2cid=246373889 |access-date=9 October 2022 |archive-date=10 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221010231650/http://liu.diva-portal.org/smash/record.jsf?pid=diva2%3A1632719&dswid=2554 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Pääbo |first=Svante |title=Neanderthal man: in search of lost genomes |date=2014 |isbn=978-0-465-02083-6 | publisher=Basic Books (AZ) |location=New York |oclc=862400377}}</ref> In this context, Svante Pääbo was able to show that the [[TKTL1]] gene discovered by [[Johannes F. Coy]] has a single amino acid substitution in Neanderthals compared to modern humans. This change probably influenced neuronal development and may have contributed to the difference in brain structure between Neanderthals and Homo sapiens.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pinson |first1=Anneline |last2=Xing |first2=Lei |last3=Namba |first3=Takashi |last4=Kalebic |first4=Nereo |last5=Peters |first5=Jula |last6=Oegema |first6=Christina Eugster |last7=Traikov |first7=Sofia |last8=Reppe |first8=Katrin |last9=Riesenberg |first9=Stephan |last10=Maricic |first10=Tomislav |last11=Derihaci |first11=Razvan |last12=Wimberger |first12=Pauline |last13=Pääbo |first13=Svante |last14=Huttner |first14=Wieland B. |date=2022-09-09 |title=Human TKTL1 implies greater neurogenesis in frontal neocortex of modern humans than Neanderthals |journal=Science |volume=377 |issue=6611 |article-number=eabl6422 |doi=10.1126/science.abl6422 |issn=1095-9203 |pmid=36074851}}</ref>

}}.</ref> He and his team also concluded that there was probably interbreeding between Neanderthals and Eurasian (but not Sub-Saharan African) humans.<ref name=bbc05062010>{{cite news |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/science/nature/8660940.stm |title=Neanderthal genes 'survive in us' |year=2010 |publisher=[[BBC]] |access-date=7 May 2010 |first=Paul |last=Rincon |archive-date=14 August 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120814082148/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/science/nature/8660940.stm |url-status=live }}</ref> There is general mainstream support in the scientific community for this theory of [[interbreeding between archaic and modern humans]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Lalueza-Fox | first1 = C | last2 = Gilbert | first2 = MTP | year = 2011 | title = Paleogenomics of Archaic Hominins | journal = Current Biology | volume = 21 | issue = 24| pages = R1002–R1009 | doi=10.1016/j.cub.2011.11.021| pmid = 22192823 | s2cid = 14371551 | doi-access = free| bibcode = 2011CBio...21R1002L }}</ref> This admixture of modern human and Neanderthal genes is estimated to have occurred roughly between 50,000 and 60,000 years ago, in the Middle East.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wong |first1=Kate |title=Neandertal Genome Study Reveals That We Have a Little Caveman in Us |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/neandertal-genome-study-r/ |website=Scientific American |language=en |access-date=11 October 2022 |archive-date=11 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221011002957/https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/neandertal-genome-study-r/ |url-status=live }} "By way of explanation, the investigators suggest that the interbreeding occurred in the Middle East between 45,000 and 80,000 years ago, before moderns fanned out to other parts of the Old World and split into different groups."</ref>

In 2014, he published the book ''[[Neanderthal Man: In Search of Lost Genomes]]'' where he, in the mixed form of a memoir and popular science, tells the story of the research effort to map the Neanderthal genome combined with his thoughts on human evolution.<ref name=forbes>Peter Forbes (20 February 2014) [https://www.theguardian.com/books/2014/feb/19/neanderthal-man-search-lost-genomes-svante-paabo Neanderthal Man: In Search of Lost Genomes by Svante Pääbo – review] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211201210648/https://www.theguardian.com/books/2014/feb/19/neanderthal-man-search-lost-genomes-svante-paabo |date=1 December 2021 }}</ref><ref>Simon Underdown (3 April 2014) [http://www.timeshighereducation.co.uk/books/neanderthal-man-in-search-of-lost-genomes-by-svante-pbo/2012342.article Neanderthal Man: In Search of Lost Genomes, by Svante Pääbo] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714164849/http://www.timeshighereducation.co.uk/books/neanderthal-man-in-search-of-lost-genomes-by-svante-pbo/2012342.article |date=14 July 2014 }} ''[[Times Higher Education]]''. Retrieved 1 July 2014.</ref>

In 2020, [[Hugo Zeberg]] and Svante Pääbo determined that more severe impacts upon victims of the [[COVID-19]] disease, including the vulnerability to it and the incidence of the necessity of hospitalisation, have been associated via DNA analysis to be expressed in genetic variants at chromosomal region 3, features that are associated with European [[Neanderthal]] heritage. That structure imposes greater risks that those affected will develop a more severe form of the disease.<ref name=Neanderthal>[https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2020/09/200930094758.htm The ancient Neanderthal in severe COVID-19] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210504173608/https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2020/09/200930094758.htm |date=4 May 2021 }}, ''[[Science News]]'', 30 September 2020. Retrieved 13 December 2020.</ref> The findings were described in a Nature article with Hugo Zeberg from [[Karolinska Institute]]t and Svante Pääbo from the Max Planck Institute.<ref name=Neanderthal />

{{As of|2022|10}}, Pääbo has an [[h-index]] of 167 according to [[Google Scholar]]<ref name=gs /> and of 133 according to [[Scopus]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.scopus.com/authid/detail.uri?authorId=7006151134|title=Scopus preview – Pääbo, Svante – Author details – Scopus|website=scopus.com|access-date=16 October 2021|archive-date=3 October 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221003134601/https://www.scopus.com/authid/detail.uri?authorId=7006151134|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Awards and honours ===
[[File:Svante Paabo and Fumio Kishida 20230201 1.jpg|thumb|200px|Pääbo showed the medal of [[Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine]] to [[Fumio Kishida]] (1 February 2023).]]
In 1992, he received the [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Prize]] of the [[Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft]], which is the highest honour awarded in German research. Pääbo was elected a member of the [[Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences]] in 2000, and in 2004 was elected an international member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Member Directory: Svante Pääbo|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/svante-paabo-tgn0r6/|access-date=3 December 2022|archive-date=28 November 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221128090055/http://www.nasonline.org/member-directory/members/20007508.html|url-status=live}}</ref> He received the [[Ernst Schering Prize]] in 2003. In 2005, he received the prestigious [[Louis-Jeantet Prize for Medicine]].<ref name="Louis-Jeantet Prize" /> In 2008, Pääbo was added to the members of the Order [[Pour le Mérite for Sciences and Arts]]. In the same year, he received the Golden Plate Award of the [[Academy of Achievement|American Academy of Achievement]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Golden Plate Awardees of the American Academy of Achievement|website=achievement.org|publisher=[[American Academy of Achievement]]|url=https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#science-exploration|access-date=13 July 2020|archive-date=15 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161215023909/https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#science-exploration|url-status=live}}</ref> In October 2009, the [[Foundation For the Future]] announced that Pääbo had been awarded the 2009 [[Kistler Prize]] for his work isolating and sequencing ancient DNA, beginning in 1984 with a 2,400-year-old mummy.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.futurefoundation.org./awards/kpr_2009_paabo.htm |title=Foundation For the Future has selected Dr. Svante Pääbo as the 2009 winner of the Kistler Prize. |access-date=27 July 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110726072228/http://www.futurefoundation.org/awards/kpr_2009_paabo.htm |archive-date=26 July 2011 }}</ref> In June 2010, the [[Federation of European Biochemical Societies]] (FEBS) awarded him the Theodor Bücher Medal for outstanding achievements in Biochemistry and Molecular Biology.<!-- the following archived URL goes wrong place. Checked September 2021 --><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.febs.org/index.php?id=129|title=FEBS MEDALS: The Theodor Bücher Lecture and Medal|access-date=27 July 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110726052213/http://www.febs.org/index.php?id=129|archive-date=26 July 2011}}</ref> In 2013, he received [[Gruber Prize in Genetics]] for groundbreaking research in [[evolutionary genetics]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mpg.de/6956763/Gruber_Genetics_Prize_2013|title=Gruber Genetics Prize for Svante Pääbo|work=MAX-PLANCK-GESELLSCHAFT|access-date=6 April 2013|archive-date=17 March 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130317212827/http://www.mpg.de/6956763/Gruber_Genetics_Prize_2013|url-status=live}}</ref> In 2014, Pääbo was awarded the Swedish [[:sv:Learning Ladder Prize]]. In June 2015, he was awarded the degree of DSc (honoris causa) at [[NUI Galway]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nuigalway.ie/about-us/news-and-events/news-archive/2015/june2015/one-of-worlds-most-influential-scientists-to-speak-at-nui-galway.html |title=ONE OF WORLD'S MOST INFLUENTIAL SCIENTISTS TO SPEAK AT NUI GALWAY |access-date=13 June 2015 |archive-date=16 June 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150616010355/http://www.nuigalway.ie/about-us/news-and-events/news-archive/2015/june2015/one-of-worlds-most-influential-scientists-to-speak-at-nui-galway.html |url-status=live }}</ref> He was elected a [[Foreign Member of the Royal Society]] in 2016,<ref name=frs>{{cite web |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160429121416/https://royalsociety.org/people/svante-paabo-12888 |archive-date=29 April 2016 |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/svante-paabo-12888 |publisher=[[Royal Society]] |location=London |year=2016 |title=Svante Paabo |url-status=live}} One or more of the preceding sentences incorporates text from the royalsociety.org website where: {{blockquote|"All text published under the heading 'Biography' on Fellow profile pages is available under [[Creative Commons license|Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License]]." --{{cite web |url=https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies |title=Royal Society Terms, conditions and policies |access-date=2016-03-09 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150925220834/https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies |archive-date=25 September 2015}}}}</ref> and in 2017, was awarded the [[Dan David Prize]]. In 2018, he received the [[Princess of Asturias Awards]] in the category of Scientific Research and the [[Körber European Science Prize]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=All prizewinners |url=https://koerber-stiftung.de/en/projects/koerber-european-science-prize/all-prizewinners/ |access-date=2025-01-07 |website=Körber-Stiftung |language=en}}</ref> in 2020 the [[Japan Prize]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.japanprize.jp/en/press.html|title=The Japan Prize Foundation|website=japanprize.jp|access-date=16 October 2021|archive-date=4 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210204194053/https://www.japanprize.jp/en/press.html|url-status=live}}</ref> in 2021 the [[Massry Prize]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://keck.usc.edu/massry-prize/current-laureates|title=Current Laureates|access-date=1 December 2021|archive-date=1 December 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211201115606/https://keck.usc.edu/massry-prize/current-laureates|url-status=live}}</ref> and in 2022 the [[Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2022/summary/|title=The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2022|publisher=Nobel Foundation|access-date=3 October 2022|archive-date=3 October 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221003100332/https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2022/summary/|url-status=live}}</ref> for sequencing the first Neanderthal genome.<ref name="ReutersNobel" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Saplakoglu |first=Yasemin |date=2022-10-03 |title=Extinct Human Genomes Studies Win Nobel Prize for Medicine 2022 |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/extinct-human-genomes-studies-win-nobel-prize-for-medicine-2022-20221003/ |access-date=2025-10-14 |website=[[Quanta Magazine]]}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Pääbo wrote in his 2014 book ''[[Neanderthal Man: In Search of Lost Genomes]]'' that he is [[bisexual]]. He assumed he was gay until he met [[Linda Vigilant]], an American [[primatologist]] and geneticist whose "boyish charms" attracted him. "I had many relationships with men, but I also had girlfriends now and again". They have co-authored many papers, are married and raising a son and a daughter together in [[Leipzig]].<ref name="Sexuality">{{Cite web|url=https://geneticliteracyproject.org/2014/03/06/sexy-science-neanderthals-svante-paabo-and-the-story-of-how-lust-shaped-modern-humans/|publisher=Genetic Literary Project|title=Sexy Science: Neanderthals, Svante Pääbo and the story of how sex shaped modern humans|first=Tabitha M.|last=Powledge|work=Genetic Literacy Project |date=6 March 2014|access-date=3 August 2019|archive-date=22 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211122224221/https://geneticliteracyproject.org/2014/03/06/sexy-science-neanderthals-svante-paabo-and-the-story-of-how-lust-shaped-modern-humans/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="PersonalLife">{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2011/08/15/sleeping-with-the-enemy |title=Sleeping with the Enemy |magazine=The New Yorker |date=8 August 2011 |last1=Kolbert |first1=Elizabeth }}</ref><ref name=lostgenomes>{{cite book|last1=Pääbo|first1=Svante|title=Neanderthal Man: In Search of Lost Genomes|date=2014|publisher=Basic Books|isbn=978-0-465-02083-6}}</ref>
